title: Order written
principle: The books in the order scholars think they were written — one framework, the critical consensus, with its date on every day.

source.name: “Dating the Bible”, Wikipedia (Tables I, II and IV), which tables the dates most widely held in critical scholarship, citing Brown, Coogan, Collins, Carr, Day, Nelson and others
source.licence: CC BY-SA 4.0 (dates used as facts; no text reproduced)

caveat: One framework’s dating. Scholars disagree, sometimes by centuries: traditional datings put the Torah under Moses and most letters earlier. The framework is named so you can weigh it.
sequence: Amos: first half of the 8th century BCE.
Hosea: second half of the 8th century BCE.
Nahum: the 7th century BCE, before Nineveh fell in 612.
Zephaniah: the reign of Josiah, about 649–609 BCE.
Deuteronomy: its core of laws in the 7th century BCE, extended in the early 6th and again in the Persian period.
Habakkuk: possibly shortly before Carchemish, 605 BCE.
Jeremiah: active in the last decade of the 7th century and the first decades of the 6th; the Hebrew version later.
Obadiah: around the fall of Jerusalem, 586 BCE.
Ezekiel: visions dated 593–571 BCE, in Babylon.
Isaiah 40–55, “Second Isaiah”: in Babylon, around the middle of the 6th century BCE.
Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings — the “Deuteronomistic history” — completed in the exile, 586–539 BCE.
Psalms 1–89: a possible early collection ending at Psalm 89; the first two-thirds of the Psalter is mostly pre-exilic.
Isaiah 56–66, “Third Isaiah”: Jerusalem, immediately after the exile.
Haggai: self-dated to Darius’s second year, 520 BCE.
Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers: their present form in the Persian period, after the exile.
Malachi: the 5th century BCE, near the missions of Nehemiah and Ezra.
Zechariah 9–14: the 5th century BCE or later.
Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song: the 4th or 3rd century BCE, possibly earlier.
Ezra–Nehemiah: perhaps as late as 300–200 BCE in its final form.
Psalms 90–150: most of the final third of the Psalter, in the Hellenistic period.
Jonah: Persian or Hellenistic, no later than the 2nd century BCE.
1 Thessalonians: about 51 CE, among the earliest letters.
2 Thessalonians: about 51 CE if Paul’s; after 70 if not. Placed with the first.
Galatians: about 48 or 55 CE, depending on which Galatia.
Philippians and Philemon: about 54–55 CE, from an imprisonment.
The letters of John: about 90–110 CE.
Jude: uncertain; before 2 Peter, which uses it.
2 Peter: about 110 CE, apparently the latest writing in the New Testament.
